How the Internet Works.code: DNS, IP addresses, routers, ISPs, and the client-server model.

HTTP Protocol.code: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3; request/response cycle; headers, methods, status codes.

REST API Design.code: Resources, HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), status codes, versioning.

DNS.code: A, CNAME, MX records; TTL; DNS propagation.

TCP/IP.code: Three-way handshake, ports, sockets, connection lifecycle.

Node.js Runtime.code: Event loop, non-blocking I/O, Node.js built-in modules (fs, path, http).

Express.js.code: Routing, middleware, request/response handling, error handling.

Python Backend.code: Django, Flask, FastAPI - ORM, routing, middleware.

Go Backend.code: net/http, gorilla/mux, Gin framework, concurrency patterns.

Relational Databases.code: PostgreSQL, MySQL - tables, indexes, joins, transactions, ACID.

Query Optimization.code: EXPLAIN, query plans, index usage, connection pooling.

Data Caching.code: Redis, Memcached, cache-aside, write-through, cache invalidation.

Migrations.code: Version-controlled schema changes, rollbacks, seeding data.

JWT (JSON Web Tokens): JWT is a compact, URL-safe token format for transmitting claims between parties. It consists of three parts: header (algorithm, type), payload (claims like user_id, role, exp), and signature (verified with a secret or key pair). JWTs are stateless — the server doesn't need to store session data, but they can't be revoked without a blocklist.

Session-Based Auth.code: Session IDs, cookies, session stores (Redis, DB).

OAuth 2.0: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that allows third-party apps to access user data without sharing passwords. It involves authorization server, resource server, and client. Grant types include Authorization Code (most common), Client Credentials (machine-to-machine), Implicit (legacy), and Refresh Token. Used by Google, GitHub, and Facebook login systems.

Security Best Practices.code: Password hashing (bcrypt), rate limiting, input validation, XSS/CSRF prevention.

API Keys.code: Key generation, rotation, rate limiting per key.

Basic Authentication: Basic Authentication is the simplest HTTP authentication method. The client sends the username and password encoded in Base64 in the Authorization header. It's insecure over plain HTTP (easily decoded) and should only be used over HTTPS. Typically paired with session tokens or API keys for modern applications.
Session & Cookie Auth: Session-based authentication uses server-side sessions identified by a cookie. When a user logs in, the server creates a session, stores it (in memory, Redis, or database), and sends the session ID as a cookie. The browser sends the cookie with each request. Provides easy revocation (delete the session) but requires server-side storage.
API Security Best Practices: API security involves multiple layers: rate limiting (prevent abuse), input validation (sanitize all inputs), HTTPS everywhere, proper authentication/authorization (least privilege principle), CORS configuration, request size limits, SQL injection prevention (parameterized queries), XSS protection, CSRF tokens, and security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options).

# API security checklist:
# [ ] HTTPS enforced (HSTS header)
# [ ] Rate limiting (100 req/min per user)
# [ ] Input validation & sanitization
# [ ] Parameterized queries (no raw SQL)
# [ ] CORS whitelist (not *)
# [ ] Authentication on all endpoints
# [ ] Role-based access control (RBAC)
# [ ] Audit logging
# [ ] Security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options)
# [ ] Request size limits

GraphQL.code: Schema definition, resolvers, queries, mutations, subscriptions.

gRPC.code: Protocol buffers, service definitions, streaming, HTTP/2.

API Versioning.code: URL versioning, header versioning, content negotiation.

Rate Limiting.code: Token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window; per-user, per-IP.

Unit Testing.code: Jest, Mocha, Vitest; mocking, stubbing, assertions.

Integration Testing.code: Supertest for HTTP, database test containers, API integration tests.

End-to-End Testing.code: Cypress, Playwright; full user journey testing.

Docker.code: Dockerfiles, images, containers, docker-compose, multi-stage builds.

CI/CD.code: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins; automated testing and deployment.

Cloud Deployment.code: AWS (EC2, Lambda, ECS), GCP (Cloud Run, GKE), Azure (App Service).

Scalability Patterns.code: Horizontal vs vertical scaling, load balancing, database sharding.

Microservices.code: Service decomposition, inter-service communication, API gateways.

Message Queues.code: RabbitMQ, Kafka, Redis streams; producers, consumers, topics.

Caching Strategies.code: CDN, application cache, database cache; cache invalidation strategies.

Database Sharding.code: Hash-based, range-based sharding; rebalancing, query routing.

Consensus Algorithms.code: Raft, Paxos, Zab; leader election, log replication.

How the Internet Works: The internet is a global network of interconnected computers that communicate using standardized protocols. Data is broken into packets, routed through multiple nodes, and reassembled at the destination. Key concepts include IP addresses, DNS, TCP/IP, and the client-server model.
What is HTTP: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the foundation of data communication on the web. It's a request-response protocol where clients send requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to servers, which return status codes (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error) and response bodies.
DNS & How It Works: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (google.com) into machine-readable IP addresses (142.250.190.46). It's a hierarchical system with root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative nameservers. DNS resolution involves recursive queries that cache results for performance.
What is Hosting: Web hosting is a service that stores your website files on a server and makes them accessible via the internet. Types include shared hosting (multiple sites on one server), VPS (virtual private server), dedicated hosting (physical server for one client), and cloud hosting (scalable resources across multiple servers).
Browsers & How They Work: Browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) are user agents that fetch, render, and display web content. The browser engine parses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, constructs the DOM and CSSOM trees, performs layout calculations, and paints pixels to screen. Key components include the rendering engine, JavaScript engine (V8, SpiderMonkey), and networking stack.
What is a Domain Name: A domain name is a unique, human-readable address that identifies a website on the internet. Domain structure includes TLD (top-level domain like .com, .org), second-level domain (the name you choose), and subdomains (like www or blog). Domains are registered through registrars and must be renewed periodically.

Git Basics: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code during development. It allows multiple developers to work simultaneously, maintains a complete history of changes, and enables branching/merging. Key concepts: repositories, commits, branches, staging area, and remote tracking.

git init                    # Initialize a new repo
git add .                    # Stage all changes
git commit -m "message"     # Commit staged changes
git branch feature          # Create a branch
git checkout feature        # Switch to branch
git merge feature           # Merge branch into current
git log --oneline           # View commit history
GitHub: GitHub is a cloud-based platform for hosting Git repositories. It provides collaboration features like pull requests, code reviews, issue tracking, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, GitHub Pages for static hosting, and project management tools. It's the largest host of source code worldwide, owned by Microsoft.

# Typical GitHub workflow:
# 1. Fork a repository
# 2. Clone to local machine
# 3. Create a feature branch
# 4. Make changes and commit
# 5. Push to your fork
# 6. Open a Pull Request
# 7. Code review and discussion
# 8. Merge to main branch
GitLab: GitLab is a DevOps platform that provides Git repository management, CI/CD pipelines, container registry, and project planning tools. It offers both cloud-hosted (GitLab.com) and self-managed (GitLab CE/EE) options. Key differentiators: built-in CI/CD with .gitlab-ci.yml, auto DevOps, and integrated monitoring.

// .gitlab-ci.yml example:
stages:
  - test
  - build
  - deploy

unit-tests:
  stage: test
  script:
    - npm install
    - npm test

build-image:
  stage: build
  script:
    - docker build -t myapp .
Repo Hosting Services: Beyond GitHub and GitLab, other repository hosting services include Bitbucket (Atlassian, integrates with Jira), SourceForge (one of the oldest), and self-hosted options like Gitea and Gogs. Each offers varying features for code review, access control, and integrations with CI/CD and project management tools.

# Choosing a hosting service:
# GitHub:   Largest community, Actions, Pages
# GitLab:   Built-in CI/CD, self-hostable
# Bitbucket: Jira integration, free private repos
# Gitea:    Lightweight, self-hosted, open source

PostgreSQL: PostgreSQL is a powerful, open-source object-relational database known for reliability, feature robustness, and performance. It supports advanced data types, full-text search, JSON/JSONB, indexing (B-tree, Hash, GiST, GIN), transactions with ACID compliance, and extensibility through custom functions and extensions like PostGIS.
MySQL: MySQL is a widely-used open-source relational database management system, popular for web applications (especially with LAMP/LEMP stacks). It offers InnoDB (transactional, foreign keys) and MyISAM (full-text search) storage engines, replication support, and strong performance for read-heavy workloads.

-- MySQL example
CREATE TABLE products (
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    category_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (category_id) REFERENCES categories(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Index for fast lookup
CREATE INDEX idx_products_category
ON products(category_id);
SQL & Querying: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for managing relational databases. Core operations include SELECT (retrieve), INSERT (add), UPDATE (modify), DELETE (remove). Advanced features include JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL), subqueries, aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG), GROUP BY, HAVING, and window functions.

-- Advanced SQL query
SELECT
    u.name,
    COUNT(o.id) AS order_count,
    SUM(o.total) AS total_spent,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(o.total) DESC) AS rank
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY u.id, u.name
HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 5
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
Normalization: Database normalization is the process of organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve integrity. Normal forms include 1NF (atomic values), 2NF (no partial dependencies), 3NF (no transitive dependencies), and BCNF (every determinant is a candidate key). Denormalization is sometimes used for read performance optimization.

-- Normalization example
-- UNNORMALIZED (0NF):
-- Orders: order_id, customer_name, items (comma-separated)

-- 1NF: Atomic values
-- OrderItems: order_id, customer_name, item_name

-- 2NF: Remove partial dependencies
-- Orders: order_id, customer_name
-- OrderItems: order_id, item_name

-- 3NF: Remove transitive dependencies
-- Orders: order_id, customer_id
-- Customers: customer_id, customer_name
-- OrderItems: order_id, item_name
ACID Transactions: ACID is a set of properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably. Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state transitions), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data persists). Isolation levels range from Read Uncommitted (dirty reads) to Serializable (full isolation).
Database Indexes: Indexes are data structures (B-tree, Hash, GiST) that speed up data retrieval at the cost of slower writes and increased storage. A primary key automatically gets a unique index. Composite indexes (multiple columns) must follow leftmost prefix rule. Use EXPLAIN to analyze query plans and find missing indexes.

-- Index creation strategies
CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email);

-- Composite index (column order matters!)
CREATE INDEX idx_state_city
ON addresses(state, city);

-- This query uses the index:
SELECT * FROM addresses
WHERE state = 'CA' AND city = 'SF';

-- This might NOT use the index:
SELECT * FROM addresses
WHERE city = 'SF';  -- skips leftmost column
Sharding & Scaling: Database scaling strategies include vertical scaling (more powerful hardware) and horizontal scaling (distributing data across multiple servers). Sharding partitions data across databases based on a shard key (e.g., user_id hash). Other approaches include read replicas for read-heavy workloads, and connection pooling for managing many concurrent connections.

-- Sharding strategies:
-- Range-based: users 1-10000 on Shard A, 10001-20000 on Shard B
-- Hash-based: shard = hash(user_id) % N
-- Directory-based: lookup table maps keys to shards
-- Geographic: users in US on Shard US, EU on Shard EU

-- Challenges:
-- Cross-shard queries are expensive
-- Rebalancing when adding shards is hard
-- JOINs across shards require app-level logic
Database Design & Modeling: Database design involves creating an efficient schema that represents the problem domain. Start with an Entity-Relationship Diagram (ERD), identify entities, attributes, and relationships (1:1, 1:M, M:N). Consider query patterns, access paths, and use cases. Tools like draw.io, dbdiagram.io, and MySQL Workbench help visualize schemas.

-- Database design process:
-- 1. Requirements analysis
-- 2. Conceptual design (ERD)
-- 3. Logical design (schema)
-- 4. Physical design (indexes, partitions)
-- 5. Normalization review
-- 6. Performance optimization

-- Key questions:
-- What queries will be most frequent?
-- What's the read/write ratio?
-- What are the data growth patterns?

MongoDB: MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database that stores data in flexible, JSON-like BSON documents. It uses a sharded cluster architecture for horizontal scaling, replica sets for high availability, and the aggregation pipeline for data processing. Best suited for flexible schemas, rapid iteration, and hierarchical data.
Redis: Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, and message broker. It supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, bitmaps, and streams. Key features: sub-millisecond latency, pub/sub messaging, Lua scripting, persistence (RDB/AOF), and built-in replication. Ideal for caching, session storage, and real-time analytics.

// Redis commands
SET user:1 '{"name":"Alice"}'
GET user:1
EXPIRE user:1 3600  # TTL 1 hour

// Data structures
LPUSH queue task1        # List
SADD tags:1 'backend'    # Set
ZADD leaderboard 1000 'Alice'  # Sorted Set

// Pub/Sub
SUBSCRIBE notifications
PUBLISH notifications 'New message'
Cassandra: Apache Cassandra is a distributed NoSQL database designed for high availability and linear scalability with no single point of failure. It uses a peer-to-peer architecture, tunable consistency levels, and the Cassandra Query Language (CQL). Best for write-heavy workloads, time-series data, and applications requiring multi-region deployment.

-- Cassandra CQL
CREATE TABLE user_timeline (
    user_id UUID,
    tweet_id TIMEUUID,
    content TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, tweet_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (tweet_id DESC);

-- Consistency levels:
-- ONE:        Fast but might read stale data
-- QUORUM:     Majority of replicas must respond
-- ALL:        All replicas must respond (slowest)
-- LOCAL_QUORUM: Quorum within a datacenter
Elasticsearch: Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It provides near-real-time full-text search, structured search, aggregations, and analytics. Data is stored as JSON documents in indexes, which are sharded across nodes. Commonly used for log analysis (ELK stack), application search, and observability.

REST APIs: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked applications. It uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to perform CRUD operations on resources identified by URLs. REST APIs should be stateless, use proper HTTP status codes, and support pagination, filtering, and versioning.

// REST API design
GET    /api/users          # List users
POST   /api/users          # Create user
GET    /api/users/:id      # Get user by ID
PUT    /api/users/:id      # Replace user
PATCH  /api/users/:id      # Update user fields
DELETE /api/users/:id      # Delete user

// Response
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "Alice",
  "email": "alice@example.com"
}
GraphQL: GraphQL is a query language for APIs developed by Meta. Clients request exactly the data they need, reducing over-fetching and under-fetching. A single endpoint (/graphql) handles all operations. Type system defines the schema, resolvers fetch data from various sources. Supports queries, mutations, and subscriptions for real-time data.
gRPC: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework by Google that uses Protocol Buffers for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport. It supports bidirectional streaming, flow control, and multiplexing. Service definitions are written in .proto files, generating client and server code in multiple languages. Ideal for microservices communication.
WebSockets: WebSockets provide full-duplex communication over a single TCP connection, enabling real-time data exchange. Unlike HTTP request-response, the server can push data to clients. Used for chat apps, live notifications, collaborative editing, and gaming. Libraries like Socket.IO add fallback transports and room management.
OpenAPI / Swagger: OpenAPI (formerly Swagger) is a standard for describing REST APIs using a YAML or JSON specification. It defines endpoints, request/response schemas, authentication, and error codes. Tools like Swagger UI generate interactive documentation, and code generators create client SDKs and server stubs automatically.

# OpenAPI 3.0 specification
openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: User API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /users:
    get:
      summary: List all users
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Successful response
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'

Caching Strategies: Caching stores frequently accessed data in a fast storage layer to reduce latency and database load. Common strategies include: Cache-Aside (application checks cache first), Read-Through (cache layer fetches from DB on miss), Write-Through (write to cache AND DB simultaneously), Write-Behind (async write to DB), and Cache Eviction policies (LRU, TTL, FIFO).
Redis as Cache: Redis is the most popular caching solution due to its in-memory performance and rich data structures. Common caching patterns include: session storage, database query result caching, page caching (full HTML), rate limiting counters, leaderboards, and distributed locks. Redis Cluster provides automatic sharding for large-scale deployments.
Content Delivery Networks: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a distributed network of servers that delivers cached static content (images, CSS, JS, videos) from locations geographically closer to users. Leading providers include Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Fastly, and Akamai. CDNs reduce latency, offload origin servers, and provide DDoS protection. Dynamic content can also be accelerated through edge computing.

# CDN workflow:
# 1. User requests example.com/image.png
# 2. DNS resolves to nearest CDN edge server
# 3. Edge server checks cache
# 4. Cache HIT -> Serve directly
# 5. Cache MISS -> Fetch from origin, cache, serve
# 6. Subsequent requests are fast!

# Cache-Control headers control behavior:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
HTTP Caching: HTTP caching allows browsers and proxies to store responses and reuse them. Cache-Control directives (max-age, no-cache, no-store, public, private) and ETags/Last-Modified headers control caching behavior. Conditional requests with If-None-Match (ETag) or If-Modified-Since allow servers to return 304 Not Modified instead of full responses, saving bandwidth.

# HTTP caching headers

# Strong caching (browser caches for 1 year)
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# Validate with server each time
Cache-Control: no-cache
ETag: "abc123"

# Never cache sensitive data
Cache-Control: no-store, private

# Conditional request (browser sends)
If-None-Match: "abc123"
# Server responds:
# 304 Not Modified (no body) -- or --
# 200 OK with new content

Nginx: Nginx is a high-performance web server, reverse proxy, load balancer, and HTTP cache. It uses an event-driven, asynchronous architecture that handles thousands of concurrent connections with low memory usage. Common use cases: serving static files, reverse proxying to application servers, SSL termination, rate limiting, and as a gateway for microservices.
Apache: Apache HTTP Server is one of the oldest and most widely-used web servers. It uses a process-based (prefork) or threaded (worker/event) MPM architecture. Configuration is done through .htaccess files (per-directory) and httpd.conf. Supports modules for rewrites (mod_rewrite), SSL (mod_ssl), authentication, caching, and proxying.

# Apache virtual host
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName example.com
    Redirect permanent / https://example.com/
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName example.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/html

    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile /etc/ssl/certs/example.crt
    SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/ssl/private/example.key

    <Directory /var/www/html>
        AllowOverride All
    </Directory>
</VirtualHost>
Reverse Proxy: A reverse proxy sits between clients and backend servers, forwarding requests and returning responses. Benefits include: load balancing across multiple servers, SSL termination (offloading encryption), caching static content, compression, rate limiting, and hiding backend server topology. Both Nginx and HAProxy are common reverse proxy solutions.

Unit Testing: Unit testing validates individual components (functions, methods, classes) in isolation. Tests should be fast, deterministic, and independent. Follow the AAA pattern: Arrange (set up), Act (execute), Assert (verify). Mock external dependencies. Aim for high coverage on critical business logic. Use test runners like Jest, pytest, JUnit, or Go test.
Integration Testing: Integration testing verifies that different components work together correctly — database queries, API endpoints, file I/O, and third-party service interactions. Unlike unit tests, integration tests use real (or containerized) dependencies. Test the boundary between your code and external systems. Use test databases and clean up data between tests.
API / E2E Testing: End-to-end testing validates the entire system from the user's perspective. For backend APIs, this means sending real HTTP requests and verifying responses, status codes, headers, and side effects. Tools like Supertest (Node.js), pytest + requests (Python), REST Assured (Java), and Postman/Newman automate API testing.

Docker: Docker packages applications and dependencies into lightweight, portable containers that run consistently across environments. Images are built from Dockerfiles using layered filesystems. Key concepts: Dockerfile (build instructions), images (read-only templates), containers (running instances), volumes (persistent data), networks (container communication), and Docker Compose (multi-container apps).

# Dockerfile example
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
Docker Compose: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file. Each service specifies its image, ports, volumes, environment variables, and dependencies. Compose handles network creation, service discovery, and startup ordering. Essential for local development environments with multiple services (app + database + cache + queue).

# docker-compose.yml
version: '3.8'
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    depends_on:
      - db
      - redis
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/myapp

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  pgdata:
Kubernetes Basics: Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Key concepts: Pods (smallest deployable unit), Deployments (declarative updates), Services (networking abstraction), ConfigMaps/Secrets (configuration), and Ingress (external access). Kubectl is the command-line tool.

# Kubernetes manifests
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
# service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: myapp
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000

RabbitMQ: RabbitMQ is a message broker implementing AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol). Producers send messages to exchanges, which route them to queues based on bindings and routing keys. Consumers process messages from queues. Supports multiple exchange types: direct, topic, fanout, and headers. Offers message durability, acknowledgments, and dead-letter queues for reliability.
Apache Kafka: Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant data pipelines. Topics are partitioned and replicated across brokers. Producers write events, consumers read from offsets. Unlike RabbitMQ, Kafka persists all messages for a configurable retention period. Used for event sourcing, log aggregation, stream processing, and data integration at scale.

# Kafka concepts
# Topic:  A category/feed name (e.g., "orders")
# Partition: Ordered, immutable sequence of records
# Offset:  Unique ID of a record within a partition
# Broker:  A Kafka server in the cluster
# Consumer Group: Group of consumers sharing work

# CLI commands
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic orders --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2
kafka-console-producer.sh --topic orders
kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic orders --from-beginning --group my-group
Message Queue Patterns: Common messaging patterns include: Work Queues (competing consumers distribute tasks), Pub/Sub (one-to-many broadcast), RPC (request-response over queue), Event Sourcing (storing events as authoritative state), CQRS (separate read/write models), Saga Pattern (distributed transactions via compensating actions), and Dead Letter Queues (failed message handling).

# Common messaging patterns

# 1. Work Queue (Task distribution)
# Multiple consumers compete for messages
# Each message processed exactly once

# 2. Pub/Sub (Broadcast)
# One message -> multiple consumers
# Each consumer gets every message

# 3. Saga (Distributed transaction)
# Order Service: Create order -> publish OrderCreated
# Payment Service: Consume -> process payment -> publish PaymentProcessed
# Inventory Service: Consume -> reserve items -> publish InventoryReserved
# If any step fails, compensating events undo previous steps

Logging: Logging records application events for debugging, auditing, and monitoring. Structured logging (JSON format) enables machine parsing and search. Log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL) control verbosity. Centralized logging with tools like ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or Loki + Grafana aggregates logs from multiple services. Avoid logging sensitive data.
Metrics & Monitoring: Metrics are numerical measurements of system health and performance collected over time. Key categories: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services, USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources. Common metrics: request latency (p50, p95, p99), error rates, throughput, CPU/memory usage, and database query times. Prometheus collects metrics; Grafana visualizes them.

# RED Method for services:
# Rate:     Requests per second
# Errors:   Failed requests / total requests
# Duration: Latency distribution (p50, p95, p99)

# USE Method for resources:
# Utilization:  % time resource is busy
# Saturation:   Queue length / contention
# Errors:       Count of error events

# Prometheus query examples:
# Request rate: rate(http_requests_total[5m])
# Error ratio:  sum(rate(http_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
# P99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
Distributed Tracing: Distributed tracing tracks requests as they flow through multiple services in a microservices architecture. Each request gets a trace ID, and each span represents a unit of work. Tools like Jaeger, Zipkin, and OpenTelemetry provide end-to-end visibility. Helpful for identifying latency bottlenecks, error propagation, and service dependencies.
Application Performance Monitoring: APM tools provide comprehensive monitoring of application performance, including transaction traces, dependency maps, error tracking, and real-user monitoring. Popular solutions include Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, and open-source alternatives like SigNoz and Grafana Faro. APM helps identify slow queries, memory leaks, N+1 problems, and external service degradation.

# What APM tracks:
# - Transaction traces (end-to-end request paths)
# - Database query performance
# - External API call latencies
# - Error rates and stack traces
# - Memory and CPU profiles
# - Garbage collection patterns
# - Slow code paths (hotspots)
# - Service dependency maps
# - Real user experience (RUM)

Continuous Integration: CI automatically builds and tests every code change to detect integration issues early. Developers merge changes frequently (multiple times daily) into a shared branch. CI servers run automated tests, linting, type checking, and security scans. Failures are reported immediately. Tools include GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, and Travis CI.

# GitHub Actions CI workflow
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
Continuous Deployment: CD automatically deploys validated code changes to production (or staging) environments. The deployment pipeline includes building artifacts, running integration tests, deploying to staging, running smoke tests, and promoting to production with strategies like blue-green (two identical environments) or canary (gradual rollout). Rollbacks should be fast and reliable.

# CD deployment strategies

# Blue-Green:
# Blue = current production
# Green = new version
# Switch load balancer from Blue to Green
# Rollback: switch back to Blue

# Canary:
# Route 5% of traffic to new version
# Monitor error rates and latency
# Gradually increase to 25%, 50%, 100%
# Rollback: route 0% to canary

# Rolling:
# Update instances one-by-one
# Keep some running during update
# Rollback: redeploy previous version
Infrastructure as Code: IaC manages infrastructure (servers, networks, databases) through machine-readable definition files, enabling version control, reproducibility, and automation. Tools include Terraform (multi-cloud provisioning), AWS CloudFormation, Pulumi (general-purpose languages), and Ansible (configuration management). IaC eliminates manual server configuration and drift between environments.

Microservices: Microservices architecture decomposes an application into small, independent services that communicate over a network. Each service owns its data (database-per-service), can be deployed independently, and is built around a business capability. Benefits include: independent scaling, technology diversity, and smaller codebases. Challenges include: distributed complexity, data consistency, and service discovery.

# Microservices principles:
# - Single Responsibility (one business capability)
# - Database per Service (no shared databases)
# - API-first design (REST/gRPC for communication)
# - Independent deployability
# - Decentralized governance (teams choose tech)
# - Resilience (circuit breakers, retries)
# - Observability (logging, metrics, tracing)
# - Automation (CI/CD for each service)
Load Balancing: Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to ensure reliability and performance. Types: DNS load balancing (round-robin), hardware load balancers (F5), software load balancers (HAProxy, Nginx), and cloud load balancers (AWS ALB/ELB, Google Cloud LB). Algorithms include round-robin, least connections, IP hash, and weighted distribution.
Database Scaling: Scaling databases involves read replicas (offload read queries to copies), connection pooling (manage DB connections efficiently), caching layers (Redis/Memcached), partitioning (vertical/horizontal), and sharding. Read replicas improve read throughput but introduce eventual consistency. Connection poolers like PgBouncer manage thousands of concurrent connections efficiently.

# Database scaling strategies

# 1. Read Replicas
# Primary handles writes, replicas handle reads
# Eventually consistent (replication lag)

# 2. Connection Pooling
# PgBouncer: Lightweight connection pooler
# Maintains persistent connections to DB
# Apps borrow/release connections

# 3. Vertical Scaling
# Bigger instance (more CPU, RAM, IOPS)
# Simpler but has upper limits

# 4. Sharding
# Split data across multiple databases
# Each shard handles subset of data
Caching Architecture: Multi-layer caching architecture: browser cache (private), CDN (edge cache), reverse proxy/load balancer (Nginx cache), application cache (in-memory), and database cache (buffer pool). Cache invalidation strategies include TTL-based (time to live), write-through (update cache and DB), write-behind (async), and event-driven invalidation (publish cache invalidation events).

# Multi-layer caching
# Browser:         Cache-Control, ETag, Service Worker
# CDN:              Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront
# Reverse Proxy:    Nginx, Varnish (microcaching)
# Application:      Redis, Memcached
# Database:         InnoDB buffer pool, Query cache

# Cache invalidation strategies:
# TTL:        "This data expires in 5 minutes"
# Write-through: "Write to cache AND database"
# Write-behind:  "Write to cache, async write to DB"
# Event-based:   "Publish event when data changes, cache subscribes"

AI-Assisted Coding: AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) use large language models to generate, refactor, and explain code. They integrate with IDEs and support context-aware completions, test generation, bug fixing, and code review. Best practices: provide clear context, review generated code, never blindly accept, and treat AI as a pair programmer, not a replacement.

# AI-assisted coding best practices:
# - Write clear comments and function names
# - Provide examples in the context
# - Break complex tasks into smaller prompts
# - Review generated code for correctness
# - Write tests first (AI generates implementations)
# - Use AI for boilerplate, refactoring, and docs
# - Never paste sensitive data into AI tools
# - Understand what AI generates - don't black-box
Building AI Features: Backend developers integrate AI capabilities through API calls to LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) or self-hosted models (Llama, Mistral). Patterns include: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation — search documents + ask LLM), embeddings for semantic search, streaming responses for real-time chat, function calling for structured outputs, and AI agents for multi-step tasks.
Prompt Engineering: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing input prompts to get desired outputs from LLMs. Techniques include: few-shot prompting (providing examples), chain-of-thought (step-by-step reasoning), system prompts (setting behavior/role), structured output constraints (JSON mode), and temperature control (creativity vs precision). Key for building reliable AI-powered backend features.

# Prompt engineering techniques

# System message (sets behavior)
You are a code reviewer. Analyze the following
code for bugs, security issues, and performance
problems. Respond in JSON format.

# Few-shot prompting (examples)
Translate these SQL queries to MongoDB:
SQL: SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 18
MQL: db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 18 } })

SQL: <user query>
MQL:

# Chain of thought (step by step)
Let's think step by step about whether this
query will use the index...

Service Decomposition: Microservices decompose applications into small, independently deployable services. Each service owns its data and communicates via APIs. Decomposition strategies: domain-driven design with bounded contexts, business capability patterns, and strangler fig for legacy migration. Services should be loosely coupled and highly cohesive. Common pitfalls: distributed monoliths (services that require synchronous deployment), chatty communication between services, and improper service granularity. Best practices include single responsibility per service, database-per-service pattern, and API versioning from day one.
API Gateway Pattern: An API Gateway is a single entry point that routes requests to appropriate microservices. It handles cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limiting, request transformation, aggregation, and protocol translation. Popular gateways include Kong, NGINX Plus, AWS API Gateway, and Envoy. Benefits include client simplification (single endpoint), centralized security, and protocol bridging (HTTP to gRPC). Drawbacks include increased latency, potential single point of failure, and added complexity. Backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern extends this by creating dedicated gateways per client type (web, mobile, IoT).

// Kong Gateway declarative config (kong.yml)
_format_version: "3.0"
services:
  - name: user-service
    url: http://user-svc:3001
    routes:
      - name: user-routes
        paths:
          - /api/v1/users
        methods: [GET, POST, PUT, DELETE]
    plugins:
      - name: rate-limiting
        config:
          minute: 100
          policy: local
      - name: key-auth
        config:
          key_names: ["X-API-Key"]

  - name: order-service
    url: http://order-svc:3002
    routes:
      - name: order-routes
        paths:
          - /api/v1/orders

# BFF for mobile (aggregated responses)
upstreams:
  - name: mobile-bff
    targets:
      - target: mobile-bff-svc:3100
        weight: 100
Service Mesh & Sidecar Pattern: A service mesh manages microservice-to-microservice communication via a dedicated infrastructure layer. Sidecar proxies (like Envoy) are deployed alongside each service to handle traffic management, observability, and security. Istio and Linkerd are popular meshes. Features include mTLS encryption, circuit breaking, retry logic, traffic splitting (canary deployments), and distributed tracing. The sidecar handles East-West traffic (service-to-service), freeing application code from networking concerns. Adoption considerations include operational complexity, resource overhead (each sidecar consumes ~50MB RAM), and debugging challenges.

# Istio VirtualService for canary deployment
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: user-service
spec:
  hosts:
    - user-service
  http:
    - match:
        - headers:
            x-canary:
              exact: "true"
      route:
        - destination:
            host: user-service
            subset: v2
          weight: 100
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: user-service
            subset: v1
          weight: 90
        - destination:
            host: user-service
            subset: v2
          weight: 10
Event-Driven Architecture: Event-driven architecture enables asynchronous communication between services via events. Events represent state changes and are published to message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS). Services consume events asynchronously, enabling loose coupling and eventual consistency. Patterns include event sourcing (storing state changes as events), CQRS (separating read/write models), saga patterns for distributed transactions, and outbox patterns for reliable event publishing. Event schemas should be versioned and evolve compatibly using Schema Registry (Avro, Protobuf).

Distributed Tracing (OpenTelemetry): Distributed tracing tracks requests across microservice boundaries. OpenTelemetry is the industry standard for instrumenting applications to generate traces, metrics, and logs. A trace consists of spans representing individual operations. Key concepts: trace ID (propagated across services via headers), span context, parent-child relationships, and sampling (head-based vs tail-based). Tools like Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, and Zipkin visualize traces. Instrumentation can be automatic (via libraries/agents) or manual. Traces help identify latency bottlenecks, error propagation, and service dependencies.
Centralized Logging (ELK/Loki): Centralized logging aggregates logs from all services into a searchable platform. The ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) and Grafana Loki are popular solutions. Structured logging (JSON format) is essential for machine parsing. Log levels (ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG) should be consistent across services. Correlation IDs in log entries link related operations across services. Log retention policies balance storage costs with debugging needs. Best practices: avoid logging sensitive data (PII), use log sampling for high-volume services, and set up alerts on error rate thresholds.
Metrics & Alerting (Prometheus/Grafana): Metrics provide quantitative data about system behavior. Prometheus collects time-series data via pull-based scraping with metric types: counters (only increase), gauges (up/down), histograms (distribution), and summaries (quantiles). Exporters (node_exporter, postgres_exporter, custom app exporters) expose metrics on /metrics endpoints. Grafana visualizes metrics with dashboards. The RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE method (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) guide what to measure. AlertManager handles alerts with routing, inhibition, and silencing rules.

OAuth 2.1 consolidates best practices from OAuth 2.0: PKCE is required for all public clients, refresh tokens must be sender-constrained, and the implicit grant is removed. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds an identity layer via the ID token (JWT). Key flows: authorization code flow (server-side apps), device authorization flow (CLI/smart TVs), and client credentials flow (machine-to-machine). Authorization servers (Keycloak, Auth0, Supabase Auth) issue JWTs that services validate. Token introspection and revocation endpoints manage active sessions. Best practices: short-lived access tokens (15 min), longer-lived refresh tokens with rotation, and never store tokens in localStorage.
API Security Best Practices: API security protects backend services from attacks. Key measures: input validation (never trust client data), rate limiting per user/IP, CORS configuration, SQL injection prevention via parameterized queries, CSRF tokens for cookie-based auth, and proper error handling (don't leak stack traces). Security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options) should be set. API keys should be rotated regularly. Webhook signatures verify payload authenticity. Implement proper logging for security events (failed auth, rate limit hits, suspicious patterns). Regular dependency scanning (Snyk, Dependabot) catches vulnerable packages.
Secrets Management: Secrets management securely stores and rotates sensitive configuration: database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, and encryption keys. Tools include HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Kubernetes Secrets (with encryption). Best practices: never commit secrets to git, use environment variables with .env files locally, encrypt secrets at rest and in transit, rotate secrets regularly (90 days), audit secret access, and use short-lived dynamic secrets when possible. Vault's dynamic secrets generate credentials on-demand with TTL enforcement.

Unit & Integration Testing: Testing ensures backend reliability. Unit tests verify individual functions/methods in isolation (mocking external dependencies). Integration tests verify components work together (database, external APIs). Test pyramid: lots of unit tests, fewer integration tests, even fewer E2E tests. Use test fixtures and factories for consistent test data. Database tests should use transactions that roll back after each test. Mock external HTTP APIs with tools like nock or WireMock. Aim for >80% coverage on business logic, but prioritize critical paths over coverage numbers.
Performance Testing & Benchmarking: Performance testing validates backend speed and scalability. Types: load testing (expected traffic), stress testing (beyond expected), soak testing (sustained load over time), and spike testing (sudden traffic surges). Tools: k6 (modern, scriptable), Artillery (Node.js-friendly), locust (Python), wrk/ab (CLI). Key metrics: requests per second (RPS), latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99), error rate, and resource utilization (CPU, memory, I/O). Always test with production-like data volumes. Identify bottlenecks (DB queries, external API calls, serialization) before optimization.
Database Migrations & Versioning: Database migrations manage schema changes across environments. Tools like Flyway, Liquibase, and knex.js provide versioned migration files. Each migration is a forward-only change (with optional rollback). Best practices: one logical change per migration, never modify existing migrations (create a new one instead), test migrations against a copy of production data, use repeatable migrations for views/functions, and separate schema migrations from data migrations. CI/CD should run migrations as part of deployment with proper locking.

Containerization (Docker Deep Dive): Docker packages backend services with dependencies. Multi-stage builds reduce image size (from 1GB+ to <200MB for Node.js). Best practices: use specific base image versions (not 'latest'), minimize layers by combining RUN commands, use .dockerignore, run as non-root user, use health checks, and leverage layer caching. Distroless images improve security by removing package managers and shells. Alpine-based images are 5x smaller but may have compatibility issues (musl libc vs glibc). Docker Compose simplifies local development with service dependencies.

# Multi-stage Dockerfile for Node.js backend
# Build stage
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Production stage
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only what's needed
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=builder /app/package.json ./
COPY dist/ ./dist/
COPY config/ ./config/

# Security: non-root user
USER nonroot

# Health check
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["node", "dist/health.js"]

EXPOSE 3000
ENV NODE_ENV=production

CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

# .dockerignore
node_modules/
npm-debug.log
.env
.git
test/
coverage/
*.md

# Docker Compose for dev
version: '3.8'
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - '3000:3000'
    environment:
      - DB_HOST=postgres
      - REDIS_HOST=redis
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_started
  
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U app']
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
  
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

volumes:
  pgdata:
CI/CD Pipelines: CI/CD pipelines automate building, testing, and deploying backend services. Stages typically: lint/format check, unit tests, build, integration tests, security scan, deploy to staging, E2E tests, deploy to production. Use caching to speed up builds (Docker layer cache, node_modules cache). Environment-specific configuration via CI/CD variables (not in code). Approval gates for production deployments. Rollback strategies: blue-green, canary, or rollback to previous version. Git flow with trunk-based development (short-lived branches, frequent merges to main).

# GitHub Actions CI/CD for backend
name: Backend CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
      redis:
        image: redis:7-alpine
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: 'npm'
      
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run test:unit
      - run: npm run test:integration
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:testpass@localhost:5432/testdb
          REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379
  
  build-and-push:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
  
  deploy:
    needs: build-and-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: superfly/flyctl-actions/setup-flyctl@master
      - run: flyctl deploy --image ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
        env:
          FLY_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FLY_API_TOKEN }}
